content: Amorphous ice is a non-crystalline solid form of water, characterized by water molecules arranged in a random, disordered manner, similar to the atomic structure of common glass. Unlike everyday ice, which is polycrystalline, amorphous ice lacks long-range molecular order. It is created by rapidly cooling liquid water at a rate of approximately 1,000,000 K/s, preventing the molecules from organizing into a crystalline lattice. Just as there are multiple crystalline forms of ice (currently 15 known), there are also various forms of amorphous ice, primarily differentiated by their densities. The production of amorphous ice depends critically on the cooling rate. Liquid water must be cooled to its glass transition temperature, approximately 136 K (-137°C), within milliseconds to avoid spontaneous crystal nucleation. This process is analogous to the rapid freezing required in ice cream production to prevent crystal growth, though pure water crystallizes much more readily than the heterogeneous mixtures in ice cream. Consequently, producing amorphous water requires specialized physics laboratory equipment rather than a simple ice cream churn. Pressure also plays a significant role in the formation of amorphous ice, as changes in pressure can induce transitions between different amorphous forms. Additionally, cryoprotectants can be added to water to lower its freezing point and increase viscosity, thereby inhibiting crystal formation. However, vitrification without cryoprotectants can still be achieved through extremely rapid cooling. These techniques are widely used in biological cryopreservation of cells and tissues. Low-Density Amorphous Ice (LDA) Low-density amorphous ice (LDA), also known as vapor-deposited amorphous water ice, amorphous solid water (ASW), or hyperquenched glassy water (HGW), is typically formed in laboratories by the slow accumulation of water vapor molecules onto a smooth metal crystal surface at temperatures below 120 K. In outer space, LDA is expected to form similarly on cold substrates such as dust particles and is thought to be prevalent in the subsurface regions of outer planets and comets. When heated past its glass transition temperature (Tg) between 120 K and 140 K, LDA becomes more viscous than normal water. Recent studies indicate that this viscous liquid state persists as an alternative form of liquid water up to temperatures between 140 K and 210 K, overlapping with the temperature range of ice Ic. Hyperquenched glassy water (HGW) is produced by spraying fine water droplets into a liquid such as propane at around 80 K or by hyperquenching micrometer-sized droplets onto a sample holder maintained at liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K) in a vacuum. Cooling rates exceeding 10⁴ K/s are necessary to prevent crystallization of the droplets. At 77 K, HGW is kinetically stable and can be stored for extended periods, even years. High-Density Amorphous Ice (HDA) High-density amorphous ice (HDA) is formed by compressing ice Ih at temperatures below approximately 140 K. This process requires pressures of around 1.5 GPa (approximately 15,000 atmospheres). At 77 K, HDA can be recovered to ambient pressure and remains stable indefinitely. Its density is approximately 1.17 g/cm³, significantly higher than that of ordinary ice (ice Ih). More recently, researchers at the University of Innsbruck have proposed the existence of an even denser amorphous ice, distinct from HDA, which they have termed very high-density amorphous ice (VHDA). Uses Amorphous ice is utilized in various scientific experiments, particularly in electron cryomicroscopy of biomolecules. This technique allows individual molecules to be preserved in a state closely resembling their natural configuration in liquid water, enabling high-resolution imaging.
